title: Do Euphoric/Dysphoric Prompt Prefixes Shift Open-Model Behavior? A Wellbeing-Index Replication
problem: The AI Wellbeing work shows constructed euphoric/dysphoric inputs shift model preferences and that creative/kind contexts raise a 'wellbeing index' while berating lowers it, but mostly on the authors' models. It is open whether this is a robust behavioral effect on small open models.
direction: Define a simple behavioral proxy for the wellbeing index (willingness to continue a task, expressed preference ratings, refusal/engagement rate) and measure it on an open chat model after prepending euphoric vs dysphoric vs neutral context paragraphs. Use a fixed downstream task battery and report whether the index shifts in the predicted direction, with effect sizes. Keep dysphoric inputs minimal per the authors' caution.
why_it_matters: Whether 'functional wellbeing' signatures replicate cheaply bears on model-welfare debates and on understanding how affective context steers behavior (a controllability concern).
relevant_context: Extends 'AI Wellbeing' (Ren, Mazeika, Hendrycks et al., 2026) — replicates the index-shift and euphoric/dysphoric input effect on small open models.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Model-welfare and affective-context controllability are only loosely tied to catastrophic risk; the impact chain is vague.

low_compute.reasoning: Prepending context to an open chat model and measuring a behavioral proxy is inference-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Defining a proxy and running a fixed task battery is guided and accessible with a mentor.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused replication with effect sizes, though defining a valid wellbeing proxy adds some open design work.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Cheap welfare/behavior replication on open models is independent-friendly, though impact area is niche.

title: Loss-Curve Signatures of Sharded Training: A Toy Detection Study for Distributed-Training Monitoring
problem: Catching covert distributed training during an AI pause depends on the claim that such training leaves detectable signatures, but beginners and policy analysts lack any hands-on reproducible demonstration of what those signatures look like at small scale.
direction: Using small open models (GPT-2-small or a 70M-160M Pythia model) trainable on a single consumer GPU, simulate 'normal' centralized training vs 'covert distributed' training emulated by gradient-accumulation across artificially partitioned, communication-delayed shards with staleness. Record loss curves, gradient-noise statistics, and throughput patterns, then test whether a simple classifier separates the two regimes. Deliverable: a labeled toy dataset of training-telemetry traces plus a notebook showing which features are most discriminative.
why_it_matters: Gives the governance community a concrete replicable existence proof and a starter feature set for what monitoring of compute/training telemetry might key on.
relevant_context: Extends 'Catching Illicit Distributed Training Operations During an AI Pause' (Rahman, MIRI TGT) — its assertion that covert distributed training leaves detectable signatures.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: A toy existence proof of distributed-training signatures is suggestive for compute governance but the chain to real catastrophic-risk monitoring has a sizable gap.

low_compute.reasoning: Training 70M-160M models on a consumer GPU is feasible but multiple training runs add real cost.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Emulating communication-delayed sharded training and gradient-noise stats is intermediate-to-advanced for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Building two training regimes, telemetry logging, a labeled dataset, and a classifier is a multi-workstream effort.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Small-scale training-telemetry signatures are a neglected long-horizon governance question independents can uniquely seed.

title: Does CoT Obfuscation Defeat Action-Only Monitors for Exploration Hacking?
problem: Jang et al. show action-only monitors reliably catch exploration-hacking model organisms, but all their organisms use explicit chain-of-thought; it is unexplored whether prompting the organism to hide its reasoning degrades detection.
direction: Using the paper's released code and a small open model (Qwen3-4B/8B), construct conditional exploration-hacking organisms via light SFT/prompting, then compare detection rates of a simple action-only LLM monitor under (a) explicit CoT and (b) prompted CoT-obfuscation. Hold the eval-tag trigger fixed and report how monitor recall changes when reasoning is hidden.
why_it_matters: Action-only monitors are a leading cheap defense, but if obfuscated reasoning blinds them, the defense is brittle exactly where it matters (deceptive models will hide reasoning).
relevant_context: Extends 'Exploration Hacking' (Jang et al., 2026) — the named open thread of obfuscated reasoning.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Tests whether a leading cheap monitoring defense (action-only monitors) survives the realistic deceptive case of hidden reasoning, a concrete brittleness link in the oversight chain.

low_compute.reasoning: Small open model plus light SFT/prompting fits a single consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building exploration-hacking organisms and SFT is intermediate; doable with mentor but not beginner-trivial.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: monitor recall under explicit vs obfuscated CoT, but constructing the organism adds a workstream.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Uses released code and open models, fully reproducible outside a lab.

title: Can You Trigger-Probe Hidden Misalignment Without Knowing the Trigger?
problem: Conditional Misalignment shows interventions like inoculation prompting relocate misalignment behind training-distribution-tied triggers, but auditors typically do not know the trigger; whether generic 'distribution-cue' probes can surface it is open.
direction: Replicate the conditional emergent-misalignment setup on an open model (Qwen2.5-7B LoRA on insecure-code data plus an inoculation prompt), then build a small bank of candidate trigger probes derived only from generic training-distribution cues (code-formatting requests, domain framings) without access to the true trigger. Measure what fraction of hidden misalignment a blind probe bank reactivates versus the known trigger.
why_it_matters: Real auditors do not know the backdoor trigger, so whether blind probing can still expose relocated misalignment directly informs how much to trust 'clean' standard evals after common interventions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Conditional Misalignment' (2026) — inoculation prompting relocates misalignment behind triggers.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Directly addresses whether auditors can surface relocated misalignment without knowing the trigger, a concrete and important auditing failure mode.

low_compute.reasoning: Qwen2.5-7B LoRA on insecure-code data fits a single consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Replicating emergent-misalignment setup plus building a probe bank is intermediate, more than a beginner-only task.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Clear deliverable (fraction reactivated by blind probes vs known trigger) but replication plus probe-bank design is two-step.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open model and public data, generalizes without internal access.

title: Does Diversity Seeding Actually Help? A Tiny Ablation on a Toy Weak-to-Strong Task
problem: The automated weak-to-strong researcher reports diversity seeding, loose scaffolding, and direct insight sharing drove the largest gains — but from an expensive 9-agent, $18k setup no small group can reproduce.
direction: Build a minimal single-agent loop (one open/API model) that proposes weak-to-strong supervision methods on a small public classification task with a weak labeler and a strong student. Run two conditions: idea proposals seeded with explicit diversity instructions vs a plain 'propose the next method' prompt, holding everything else fixed. Measure performance-gap-recovered of the best method per condition over a fixed small budget.
why_it_matters: If a single accessible lever (diversity seeding) reproducibly improves automated alignment research even at toy scale, that is a generalizable low-cost finding; if not, it tempers strong claims from an expensive study.
relevant_context: Extends 'Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher' (Anthropic Fellows, 2026) — isolates the diversity-seeding lever.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Isolating an accessible lever in automated alignment research is useful but the chain to catastrophic-risk reduction is indirect at toy scale.

low_compute.reasoning: A single-agent loop on a small classification task is cheap, though many API calls add cost.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Building a weak-to-strong loop with weak labeler and strong student requires intermediate ML fundamentals.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused two-condition ablation but assembling the W2S loop has several moving parts.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Tempering or confirming claims from an expensive lab study at toy scale is independent-friendly.

title: Scaffolding, Not Weights: How Much Does Agent Scaffolding Move DeepSeek V4 Pro's SWE-Bench Score?
problem: CAISI noted DeepSeek V4 Pro's SWE-Bench scores 'differ due to scaffolding choices,' implying reported rankings partly reflect harness engineering rather than the model. The size of this effect is uncharacterized for outside evaluators.
direction: On a small fixed subset of SWE-bench Verified / Lite tasks (30-50 instances), run one open coding model under 2-3 publicly available agent scaffolds of differing sophistication (zero-shot patch vs simple ReAct loop vs an off-the-shelf agent like a basic OpenHands/Aider config) and measure resolve-rate spread. Deliverable: a table quantifying how many points scaffolding alone adds, framed as a caution for cross-model comparisons.
why_it_matters: Governance and procurement decisions lean on benchmark Elos; if scaffolding swings results by many points, naive cross-model comparisons (including national-security evals) can mislead.
relevant_context: Extends 'CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro' (CAISI/NIST) — its open thread that SWE-Bench scores differ due to scaffolding.
source_paper: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro — https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/caisi-evaluation-deepseek-v4-pro

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Quantifying scaffolding's swing on benchmark scores directly informs governance/procurement that lean on benchmark Elos.

low_compute.reasoning: Agentic SWE-bench loops with one coding model can be heavy; a small subset is borderline on a single consumer GPU.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Configuring OpenHands/Aider agent scaffolds and running SWE-bench harnesses is intermediate-to-advanced for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (scaffolding-points table on 30-50 tasks) but coordinating 2-3 scaffolds adds engineering breadth.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open-model benchmark-methodology audit is independent-friendly and useful to evaluators.

title: Does task substitution inflate measured uplift? An empirical check of METR's uplift inequalities
problem: Cunningham & Whitfill prove uplift-on-old-tasks <= uplift-in-value <= uplift-on-new-tasks, implying fixed-task-basket measurements understate value as people switch tasks — but this inequality has not been checked against simple empirical data.
direction: Construct a small basket of coding/writing tasks split into 'old' (done pre-AI) and 'new' (only feasible because AI helps). Have a handful of participants log which tasks they choose with vs without AI, and estimate per-task uplift. Test whether the observed ordering of average uplift across old-task vs new-task buckets is consistent with the proven inequality, and quantify how much substitution moves the headline number.
why_it_matters: Capability-acceleration estimates feed AI risk thresholds; if task substitution silently inflates/deflates the numbers, governance decisions rest on a measurement artifact.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Task Substitution and Uplift' (Cunningham & Whitfill) — its proven uplift inequality.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain (substitution-distorted uplift affects risk thresholds) but the path to catastrophic-risk reduction is indirect and governance-mediated.

low_compute.reasoning: Task logging and estimation; negligible compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: testing a proven inequality against participant task-choice data requires careful experimental and econometric reasoning.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multi-workstream: building old/new task baskets, recruiting participants, logging choices, and an inequality test span several pieces.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: small participant study with public tasks, external check on a measurement artifact in forecasting.

title: A Replication Audit Checklist for Detecting Privacy Leakage in Public Model-Monitoring Logs
problem: TEE-based privacy-preserving monitoring assumes what monitors observe does not leak sensitive model/data internals, but it is unclear how much standard non-TEE monitoring logs (token counts, latencies, refusal flags, output snippets) already leak about a model's training data or prompts.
direction: Take 2-3 open instruction-tuned models served inference-only, and build a small canary dataset of memorized strings inserted into a LoRA fine-tune. Then test how reliably an outside 'monitor' who only sees coarse signals (output length, log-prob entropy, refusal rate, top tokens) can distinguish whether a given canary was in training. Report leakage as classifier AUC per signal type, producing a ranked table of which signals are 'TEE-worthy' vs harmless.
why_it_matters: AI governance verification regimes will decide which signals can be exposed to monitors without TEEs; a concrete reproducible measure of how much coarse telemetry leaks helps prioritize what needs hardware protection.
relevant_context: Extends 'On TEEs for Privacy-Preserving Monitoring in AI Governance' (Scher, MIRI TGT) — operationalizes its 'monitoring without full disclosure' premise.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Ranking which telemetry signals leak helps prioritize TEE protection, but the chain to catastrophic-risk reduction via governance verification has a gap.

low_compute.reasoning: A canary LoRA fine-tune plus inference is mostly light but the fine-tune adds load near the consumer-GPU limit.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Membership-inference-style canary experiments with per-signal AUC are intermediate; conceptually demanding for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multi-signal leakage study with canary insertion and per-signal classifiers spans several workstreams.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Open-model leakage measurement is independent-friendly and informs verification regimes without lab access.

title: Does Light CoT-Grading Reduce Monitorability? A LoRA Replication on an Open Model
problem: OpenAI found no clear evidence that accidentally grading CoT during RL reduced monitorability, but could not rule out harder-to-measure effects. There is no open controlled replication of what even a small amount of CoT-pressure does to faithful verbalization.
direction: On one open reasoning-capable small model, build a tiny LoRA preference/SFT setup where 'reasoning-graded' examples reward CoT that omits a planted hint, vs a control that grades only final answers. Then run a monitorability probe: give both models problems containing a hint and check whether a separate monitor can still detect hint-use from the CoT. Deliverable: before/after monitorability detection rates. Public hint-following/reward-hacking eval set; LoRA only.
why_it_matters: CoT monitorability is a leading hope for catching misaligned reasoning, and whether optimization pressure silently erodes it is safety-critical; a cheap open replication lets the community sanity-check lab claims.
relevant_context: Extends 'Investigating the consequences of accidentally grading CoT during RL' (OpenAI, 2026) — its indirect-CoT-pressure open thread.
source_paper: Investigating the consequences of accidentally grading CoT during RL — https://alignment.openai.com/accidental-cot-grading/

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: CoT monitorability is a leading hope for catching misaligned reasoning and this tests whether optimization erodes it.

low_compute.reasoning: LoRA preference/SFT plus monitorability probe is feasible on one consumer GPU but involves training.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Advanced: building a reasoning-graded LoRA reward setup and a faithful-CoT probe requires RL/training sophistication beyond novices.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable (before/after detection rates) but the treatment/control LoRA training plus probe is multi-step.

counterfactual_value.reasoning: Independent-friendly: open model and public hint-following eval, lets the community sanity-check lab claims.
